about.introduction: I got into programming because I wanted to understand the software that keeps the world running: compilers, operating systems, and database engines. That curiosity drew me to computer science, and I’m now studying Computer System Technology at Saskatchewan Polytechnic. I want to understand these systems deeply enough to build fast, efficient software of my own.
story: AI has made that curiosity even more exciting. Being able to describe the mathematical behavior of a program and work with AI to turn it into code lets me spend less time on routine implementation and explore more ambitious ideas. I’m interested in how far that can take me, especially in building high-performance software.

projects.name: Origami Lab
projects.description: An interactive paper-folding playground where flat crease patterns turn into 3D shapes.

image.alt: Origami Lab displaying a blue Miura tessellation at 65% fold with the pattern collection and paper controls

roleAndChallenge.text: The folding physics was the part I most wanted to understand. I implemented the solver from a published finite element method, using small AI-assisted numerical experiments to get comfortable with mathematics I hadn’t used before.
One stubborn bug only appeared on my phone. Tracking it down to FP16 storage precision finally got the same folds converging on both devices.

reflection.text: The demo brings that solver into a hands-on view of paper and creases. Building it taught me how much a small numerical detail can change what you see on screen.

projects.name: SQL/REPL
projects.description: A small browser-based SQL workspace for querying local files and exploring the results.

image.alt: SQL/REPL dark editor with highlighted analytics SQL and twelve query result rows

roleAndChallenge.text: I’d wanted to try something close to a compiler or interpreter, and a SQL tool felt like a manageable place to start. With DuckDB handling queries, I focused on the interface and how the database keeps track of changes.
I built a changeset algorithm around the original database snapshot, with compute and query costs in mind. It passed the existing tests for inserts, edits, and deletions.

reflection.text: Putting the editor and results side by side made the project feel complete: a place to try an idea and see what comes back. The most interesting work for me was underneath that interface, figuring out how to represent changes cleanly.

projects.name: 5D Chess · AI Spectator
projects.description: AI players take on chess with time travel and branching timelines.

image.alt: 5D Chess in its dark theme showing the two initial boards

roleAndChallenge.text: Once I discovered that 5D chess was a real game, I wanted to see what AI would make of it. I adapted an open-source game to give models the rules and board state, along with limited retrieval to help them decide what to do next.
Seeing the models use time travel and create new timelines was the payoff. Full games were expensive in tokens, so most of my testing focused on shorter runs.

reflection.text: The spectator view lets you follow those branching boards and experiment with AI players. It also made the cost of an AI experiment very tangible: each extra turn had to be worth running.

projects.name: Molecular Explorer
projects.description: A 3D viewer for exploring protein structures and other biological molecules.

image.alt: Molecular Explorer showing a three-dimensional molecular structure alongside its molecule selection menu

roleAndChallenge.text: This began as a much bigger idea: a visual library of organic chemistry reactions. The sources I found mostly offered structural diagrams, and gathering usable spatial data would have become a project of its own.
I narrowed the idea to exploring existing structures with Mol*. The result keeps the part that interested me most—being able to rotate a molecule and get a feel for its shape.

reflection.text: Changing direction helped me finish something useful. The viewer is a reminder to explore the available data early, while there’s still room for the idea to change.

projects.name: Internet Pulse
projects.description: Internet measurements mapped onto an interactive globe and world map.

image.alt: Internet Pulse globe displaying simulated network measurements and latency statistics

roleAndChallenge.text: I made Internet Pulse to try data visualization for the first time. Network measurements gave me a way to explore how geography, color, and filtering can make a dataset easier to navigate.

reflection.text: The screenshot shows the demo in simulation mode. One detail that matters when reading the map: the arcs connect measurement endpoints, not physical cables. That distinction is part of learning to make a visualization understandable as well as interesting.

technicalEvidence.title: Numerical implementation · Origami Lab
technicalEvidence.text: A research-derived FEM solver, checked with small numerical experiments and investigated across desktop and mobile. The case study explains the precision failure; the demo shows folding behavior.

technicalEvidence.title: Database state & UI · SQL/REPL
technicalEvidence.text: A browser workspace and snapshot-based changeset algorithm. The case study records passing existing insert, edit, and deletion tests; the demo shows the query interface.

softEvidence.title: Learning as I go
paragraphs: When something is unfamiliar, I break it into smaller problems I can work through. That’s how I approached the finite element method for my origami solver: I used AI-assisted experiments to understand the behavior and check my implementation before taking on the full simulation.

I also stick with problems that don’t have an obvious explanation. When the solver worked on my laptop but failed on my phone, digging through documentation helped me trace the issue to storage precision and get both working.

softEvidence.title: Knowing when to change direction
paragraphs: I’m willing to rethink an idea when I learn what it would actually take to build it. My molecular project started as a library of organic chemistry reactions, but finding usable spatial data would have turned it into a much larger research task.
I narrowed it to a viewer for existing protein structures. That kept the part I cared about—exploring chemistry visually—while giving me something I could realistically finish.

bullets: Implemented a paper-folding solver from a published finite element method, learning FEM through AI-assisted small-scale numerical experiments.
Investigated mobile convergence failures affecting roughly 30% of development test cases; traced the issue to FP16 storage precision and resolved the affected failures.
Built the UI and a snapshot-based changeset algorithm for a miniature browser database, prioritizing compute and query efficiency.
Passed the existing codebase’s insert, edit, and deletion tests; integrated with an existing SQL engine.
Adapted an open-source 5D chess game to supply rules and game state to AI players, with retrieval limited to two queries per turn under 50 ms each.
Observed time travel and timeline branching in approximately 80% of development test cases; token costs limited completed games.
